content.title: About
content.content: Flavored sunflower seeds are roasted sunflower kernels coated with natural flavorings (e.g., barbecue, smoky, cheese). They have a crunchy texture, a light salty note, and a pronounced taste characteristic of the chosen flavor. Seeds are commonly eaten as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower is one of the fastest‑growing crops; a single plant can reach up to 3 m in height within a season.
Sunflower seeds are rich in vitamin E, magnesium, and selenium.
Flavorings are usually made from natural extracts of spices, herbs, and dried fruits, without artificial colorants.
In Russia and other CIS countries, flavored seeds became a popular street snack in the 2000s.
Sunflower seeds are also processed into oil, which is considered one of the healthiest vegetable oils.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat is polyunsaturated, including omega‑6, which is important for heart health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Seeds deliver plant protein and dietary fiber, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: Vitamin E and fatty acids help keep skin moisturized and protected.

items.title: Seed allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sunflower seeds.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Seeds are calorie‑dense, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Salt and flavor additives
items.content: Excessive salt or artificial additives can be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Risk of over‑snacking
items.content: Because they are easy to eat, flavored seeds can lead to overeating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Seeds can be enjoyed straight from the bag, tossed into salads, soups, yogurts, porridge, or used in baking. They are often lightly roasted to enhance flavor. For lower sodium intake, choose unsalted versions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
